step.text:
The `square` class only handles corner radius, and the static 64px padding on the CrewMark span creates an unwanted gap when the window goes fullscreen and the traffic lights disappear. I need to remove that padding in fullscreen mode—since `square` is on `#root` which is an ancestor of the header, I could use a CSS rule, but following the project's conventions, a Tailwind variant would be cleaner. Let me check what custom variants are available.

Actually, `square` gets toggled for both fullscreen and maximized states, but they're not equivalent. On macOS, maximizing (zoom) still shows the traffic lights, so using `square` as the signal for removing padding would incorrectly strip the padding when zoomed on Mac. I need a separate signal for true fullscreen rather than conflating it with maximized. The cleanest approach is to have the main process send the actual fullscreen state separately, since right now one channel handles both fullscreen and maximized just for the corner radius purpose.

I'll restructure this minimally: the main process sends an object with both `square` (for corner radius, triggered by fullscreen or maximized) and `full` (for true fullscreen only), the preload exposes a listener that receives this shape object, and then I can apply both a `square` class and a `fullscreen` class to the document element. This lets me use Tailwind variants like `mac:fullscreen:pl-0` to handle the padding correctly.

Adding custom variants... Rather than competing CSS classes with equal specificity, I should compute the padding directly in the component based on state—that's clearer and avoids the fragility of relying on CSS load order. For the fullscreen case, the traffic lights disappear, so the logo needs to shift left to the edge instead of maintaining a gap. I'm planning to create a `useFullscreen` hook to manage this state.

Looking at how the existing theme and sound stores are structured to follow the same pattern, and I'm realizing the preload script doesn't send the initial fullscreen state on load—only when the event fires—so I need to handle that initialization gap where the shape isn't synced yet.

What changed:

- `src/main/index.ts:186` — the shape message now carries two facts, `square` and `full`. It was one flag standing for both, and only fullscreen takes the stoplights away: zooming a window on macOS keeps them, so a single flag would have pulled the mark left on a zoom too. It also fires on `did-finish-load`, so a reload while fullscreen comes back knowing it.

The `mac:` variant stays, so the platform is still decided in CSS and only the fullscreen half is decided in JS. Nothing competes for the same property, so no Tailwind ordering to depend on.

The protocol will handle score submissions from clients and broadcast the current leaderboard back, with scores also appearing as ephemeral events in chat that get trimmed out. The server will maintain the best score per player per game, keeping the top N entries per game.

Like the music controls, I'll restrict score submissions to the UI runner. For storage, I'm adding `scores: GameScore[]` directly to the crew store state rather than creating a separate games store—the snapshot will initialize it and incoming `game.scores` messages will update it, keeping everything consistent with how tools are managed.

I'm sketching out a game controller icon that works at 16 pixels. A full gamepad with all the details would be too cluttered, so I'm weighing simpler options—an arcade joystick, a two-button handheld, or a minimal gamepad with just the essential silhouette. The goal is to keep it to three marks or fewer while maintaining that soft, geometric style with rounded edges rather than sharp lines.

For the body, I'm working with a wide rounded rectangle at 19 × 15.2 pixels to stay on the keyline grid, which gives it a chunky, plump handheld console feel. I'd add a d-pad cross on the left and two button dots on the right to make it read as a controller. The challenge is that this same rounded rect body is already used for the screen, window, and terminal icons in the set, so I need to make sure the controller reads distinctly with its internal marks.

I'm weighing whether a simple rect with a cross and dots is clear enough at 16px, or if I should go with a more recognizable gamepad silhouette that has grips bulging out from the sides. The two-handled pad shape is more distinctive, though at small sizes those grips might just become nubs. I'm also considering whether an arcade joystick might be a more playful and unmistakable direction.

I think the gamepad is the strongest signal for "game," so I'm going to commit to that: a wide rounded rectangle using the 19 × 15.2 keyline with heavy corner rounding, then adding a small d-pad cross on the left and two dots on the right to complete the controller look.

On whether to fill those buttons—I'm realizing that at small sizes, outlined rings just collapse into smudges, so solid dots are actually the right call here, same reasoning as the ellipsis or the sun glyph. That gives me three marks total: the body, the cross, and the dots, which feels clean.

Now I'm working through the actual pad shape itself. A simple plus inside a rounded rectangle might work if I get the proportions right with a heavier corner radius and a slight waist. But I'm also considering a more distinctive gamepad silhouette—something with an inset at the top and grip shapes at the bottom. Let me check how the existing glyphs handle their shapes in the codebase for consistency, then I'll nail down the exact dimensions and draw it out. Sketching out the gamepad body as a path with a wide rounded rectangle base that's 19 units wide and 13 units tall, where the bottom corners extend down into grip shapes and the bottom edge curves upward in the middle to separate them.

I'm checking the tolerance on the aspect ratio — with a height of 13.5 and width of 19, the diagonal is about 16, which is 6% under the target of 17, so that should pass the icon audit. + // Something to play while you wait. The games are the app's own, they run in the
+ // side panel, and the only thing about them the crew keeps is the score: one row
+ // per person per game, their best, so a leaderboard is a table of people rather
+ // than a log of every round anyone ever played.
+ 
+ export interface GameInfo {
+   id: string
+   name: string
+   // One line for what it is, which is all a row has space for.
+   note: string
+   // What the score counts, in one word, so a column can say lines or pipes
+   // rather than points for everything.
+   unit: string
+ }
+ 
+ export const GAMES: readonly GameInfo[] = [
+   { id: 'tetris', name: 'Tetris', note: 'Stack the falling blocks', unit: 'points' },
+   { id: 'flappy', name: 'Flappy Bird', note: 'Fly through the gaps', unit: 'pipes' }
+ ]
+ 
+ export const gameFor = (gameId: string): GameInfo | null =>
+   GAMES.find(game => game.id === gameId) ?? null
+ 
+ export interface GameScore {
+   gameId: string
+   name: string
+   score: number
+   ts: number
+ }
+ 
+ // A round nobody could really have played is not a score. The ceiling is high
+ // enough that nothing anyone reaches by hand is refused and low enough that a
+ // number arriving from somewhere else cannot sit at the top of the board
+ // forever.
+ export const SCORE_LIMIT = 1_000_000
+ 
+ export function cleanGameScore(gameId: string, score: unknown): number | null {
+   if (!gameFor(gameId)) return null
+   if (typeof score !== 'number' || !Number.isFinite(score)) return null
+   const whole = Math.floor(score)
+   if (whole <= 0 || whole > SCORE_LIMIT) return null
+   return whole
+ }
+ 
+ const key = (gameId: string, name: string): string => `${gameId}\n${name.toLowerCase()}`
+ 
+ // The board for one game, best first. Two people on the same score are read in
+ // the order they got there, so whoever did it first stands higher.
+ export function boardFor(scores: GameScore[], gameId: string): GameScore[] {
+   return scores
+     .filter(one => one.gameId === gameId)
+     .sort((a, b) => b.score - a.score || a.ts - b.ts)
+ }
+ 
+ export function bestFor(scores: GameScore[], gameId: string, name: string): number {
+   const held = new Map(scores.map(one => [key(one.gameId, one.name), one]))
